News.title: Trafficking survivor pleads with Shabana Mahmood to pause 'devastating' asylum change
News.content:
Trafficking survivor pleads with Shabana Mahmood to pause 'devastating' asylum change

EXCLUSIVE: Charities warn that a new streamlined interview process - which means asylum cases with little chance of success can be dismissed faster - will mean torture survivors are at greater risk of being wrongly deported

View 2 Images Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood faces calls to pause a new streamlined interview process (Image: Dan Kitwood/PA Wire)

Controversial asylum fast-tracking rules mean torture and trafficking survivors are at greater risk of being wrongly sent back to danger, Shabana Mahmood has been warned.

‌



The Home Secretary faces calls to pause a streamlining of the interview process which means some people only get one opportunity to make their case. Campaigners say traumatised victims often need more time to open up about what they have gone through.

‌



One trafficking survivor told The Mirror the changes will be "devastating" for people like him. The Helen Bamber Foundation and Freedom From Torture have called on the Home Office to rethink the new system, which came into effect on August 3.

‌



The Home Office says it will be able to identify cases that are unlikely to succeed without multiple assessments. But the charities claim this will lead to flawed decisions and lead to further appeals further down the line. They also fear most asylum seekers will have no access to legal advice before their screening interview - meaning it is very unlikely they will understand the process and what they need to do.

MP Rupert Lowe skewered as he flaps over whether King Charles is a white British man READ MORE :

Terrorism referrals rocket as children account for one in three cases READ MORE :

View 2 Images Charities warn the new regulations will lead to a rise in wrongful refusals (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Kamena Dorling, director of policy at the Helen Bamber Foundation, said: "You cannot expect a survivor of torture or trafficking to disclose the most painful experiences of their life in a single interview. Many people arrive in the UK terrified, traumatised and deeply distrustful of authority. For survivors, disclosure is often a gradual process that takes place over weeks or months, not hours.

‌



"These changes risk creating a system where people are refused before they have had a real opportunity to explain what happened to them or provide evidence of the harm they have suffered.”

Under the new rules, laid before Parliament in July, some asylum claims will be determined without a separate substantive refugee interview. Both charities have written to the Parliament's Secondary Legislation Scrutiny Committee saying the new system could increase the risk of wrongful refusals.

Sile Reynolds, from Freedom from Torture, said: “The government should be capable of deciding asylum claims more quickly – it’s in no-one’s interest for survivors to be stuck in a backlog, unable to heal, work and move on with life. But the safety of the process and the quality of the decision must not be sacrificed in the pursuit of speed, or we run the risk of sending refugees back to torture and persecution.

‌



"The government is already getting it wrong in too many cases leading to an outrageous backlog at the appeal courts. We all want to see an end to the chaos and harm inflicted on those seeking sanctuary in the UK but this must not be at the expense of fairness and justice.”

And Chris, a survivor of trafficking supported by Helen Bamber Foundation, said: "Based on my own experience as a survivor of trafficking, these changes would be devastating. They would close the window for some people seeking asylum to tell the truth about what has happened to them.

"We are human beings, and before we can talk about our trauma, we need to feel safe and be able to trust the person asking the questions. The first interview happens very soon after arriving in a new country, when you don't know anyone or understand what will happen next.

Article continues below

"Many survivors are living with trauma, memory loss, fear and shame. You cannot switch off that trauma on demand. It takes time to build enough trust to speak about experiences like trafficking and exploitation, and many people only feel able to disclose what happened little by little."

A Home Office spokesman said: “We would reassure victims and survivors of these horrific experiences that their asylum claims will continue to be examined under the standard process.

“Merged registration is only intended for a limited number of claims from safe countries, where there is no realistic prospect of a claim being granted. This will help deliver quicker decisions, reduce lengthy periods of uncertainty, and ensure protection is granted swiftly to those who genuinely need it.”

News.title: More areas of UK likely to move into drought as fifth heatwave builds
News.content:
Sunday is forecast to be a warmer day across many areas with temperatures widely getting up to the mid to high twenties Celsius. South-east England will be even hotter where temperatures could rise as high as 33C.

After a cooler day on Monday, temperatures will then rise widely across the UK from Tuesday.

In Scotland and Northern Ireland, temperatures will typically reach the low to mid twenties.

In England and Wales, temperatures will rise into the mid to high twenties Celsius and widely across east Wales, central, eastern and southern England in excess of 30C.

The heat is set to peak on Thursday, with readings of 35C possible in south-east England.

If this happens, it will be the fourth consecutive month of 35C or more being recorded.

The threshold for declaring an official heatwave is likely to be reached widely across England and Wales, making it the fifth heatwave of the year for many.

Yellow heat health alerts are in effect for most of England until 21:00 BST on Tuesday, warning of impacts for health and social care services and an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

These are likely to be updated in the coming days as heatwave conditions develop.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
News.content:
After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?

A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.

But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.

The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.

In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a â¬150,000 (Â£128,000) fine, if convicted.

Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Ãtape forest in the Vosges region.

"Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est RÃ©publicain, the newspaper that reported the story.

Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts.

"I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.

The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.

The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.

But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances.

"The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
News.content:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"Iâm still in shock,â she adds. âThe thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" â where stars match outfits to a film's themes â Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.â

News.title: Why eclipse chasers are crossing continents for solar spectacle: 'It's like the World Cup'
News.content:
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.

For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.

Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.

It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".

But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.

News.title: Family 'devastated' as hit-and-run driver who killed boy, 13, to have early prison release
News.content:
The family of a 13-year-old boy killed in a hit-and-run say they are "devastated" after being told the driver who caused his death has had his sentence reduced.

Kaylan Hippsley died three days after being struck by a car driven by Harley Whiteman on Brecon Road in Hirwaun, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 29 February 2024.

Whiteman was originally sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and banned from driving for eight years and four months but, after Kaylan's family appealed, High Court judges increased the sentence to nine years.

Now, the family has been told Whiteman can be released under licence as early as this autumn as part of the UK government's Sentencing Act early release scheme.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning 'on the ground' - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after three hit by car
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and dangerous driving after three pedestrians were hit by a car following reports of a disturbance.

The incident happened on Stokes Croft in Bristol at about 06:30 BST, according to Avon and Somerset Police.

A spokesperson for the force said one of the pedestrians was taken to hospital, but their injuries were not considered to be life-changing or life-threatening. The two others were not seriously injured.

A man police believe to be the car's driver was treated for facial injuries after his arrest.

Thomas Street, Hepburn Road, Stokes Croft and City Road are all closed while police make enquiries, with more officers than usual in the area as investigations continue.

The Best Off Licence in Stokes Croft was also damaged in the incident.

Bristol Supt Matt Ebbs said: "We would like to assure the public we do not believe there to be any wider threat.

"Anybody with concerns is welcome to speak to officers on the ground, but we would also appeal to anybody with CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which may assist our enquiries to contact us."

News.title: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandise
News.content:
Celebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?

At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days.

It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.

While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.

Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care.

Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers.

"We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"

Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.

Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers.

Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.

News.title: Man's body found in burning car
News.content:
The body of a man has been found inside a burning car in Portadown, County Armagh.

Police were called to the scene at Harford Street in the town centre at about 22:00 BST on Saturday.

Firefighters extinguished the blaze and the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

Ch Insp Tierney, from the Police Service of Northern Ireland said the circumstances are under investigation and a post-mortem examination will be carried out to determine the cause of his death.

The cause of the car fire will also be investigated.

The vehicle's windows were smashed and it was significantly damaged by the blaze.

A neighbouring property in the street sustained scorch damage, according to police.

The officer added: "Ammunition Technical Officers (ATO) were also tasked to the scene to conduct relevant enquiries â we can confirm there is no risk to the public."

News.title: How an entire generation of young people were written off by the state
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Jerry Tolbert was just 14 when he used an imitation firearm to rob someone of their mobile phone, a silver Nokia 6280 worth £190, in what was described during his 2007 trial as an “unremarkable but serious” crime.

Despite his age and the nature of the offence, the judge decided the child in the dock, then still only 15, was dangerous and sentenced him to a draconian indefinite jail term, which has since been abolished from the statute books.

Two decades later, Tolbert was still in custody – until the Court of Appeal this year ruled the punishment was “obviously wrong”.

“It would appear that Tolbert was sentenced to, in effect, a life sentence by a judge who did not appreciate that he was dealing with a 15-year-old defendant,” a panel of judges led by Lord Justice Edis said in a scathing judgment, which concluded the sentencing process was “unacceptable and the result has been unjust”.

Tolbert’s case is one of six imprisonment for public protection (IPP) and its youth equivalent, detention for public protection (DPP) jail terms, quashed in the sweeping ruling because the courts had failed to take into account the offenders’ age and immaturity.

Another offender, Jay Davis, had served the best part of 20 years in custody for threatening someone with a pellet gun aged 19. He should have received an 18-month determinate sentence, the Court of Appeal found.

open image in gallery Chair of the CCRC Vera Baird said young offenders handed indefinite jail terms was a ‘terrible miscarriage of justice’ ( PA )

His case had been flagged by the country’s miscarriages of justice watchdog, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which is now reviewing more than 180 similar cases – with more applications arriving every week.

Its chair, Dame Vera Baird, believes it is time the government takes “wholesale” action to review or resentence those still serving the controversial jail terms.

“I think we are increasingly seeing that a lot of men who were sentenced when young have had terrible miscarriages of justice imposed upon them,” she told The Independent.

This week, new prime minister Andy Burnham announced his government would do just that – ordering a review of the jail terms as a way of tackling Britain’s prison crisis and freeing up much-needed space in Britain’s overcrowded jails.

The move was welcomed by former lord chief justice John Thomas, who said the sentences were a “stain” on the justice system, while Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said Mr Burnham’s intervention would offer “hope to the hopeless”.

Dame Vera welcomed the move but called for the CCRC, which she said was “referring as many [cases] as we can as quickly as we can” to the Court of Appeal, to be involved in the review.

The open-ended sentences – which The Independent has campaigned for more than two years to have reviewed – were outlawed in 2012, but not retrospectively. Introduced under New Labour in a bid to be tough on crime, they were handed to many repeat offenders, even if their crimes were minor. The idea was that criminals would only be released when they could prove to a Parole Board that they no longer posed a risk to the public.

More than 2,700 under-25s, including 1,495 under-21s, 17 children under 14, and even a 10-year-old, were among those who found themselves locked up without a release date.

Some 14 years after the sentence was recognised as a mistake, almost 2,400 IPP and DPP prisoners remain incarcerated. Some have served up to 22 times their original minimum term, while others are in a vicious cycle of recall, often for breaches of strict licence conditions.

But the campaigning United Group for the Reform of IPP (Ungripp) says the growing numbers of sentences now being quashed “exposes a devastating reality: an entire generation of young people was written off by the state”.

open image in gallery The Court of Appeal has quashed a string of IPP sentences ( PA Archive )

Dame Vera, who was appointed as chair of the CCRC last summer, was the Labour MP for Redcar when the sentences were first introduced in 2005. Even then, she thought the project was a “risky manoeuvre”.

“But who could expect that it would last this long and cause so much damage, which I’m afraid it has done,” she added. “It’s very odd that we’re left over with a lot of people who are still stuck on something that we all accept should never have been implemented.”

Despite 96 prisoners taking their own lives in custody after losing hope of ever getting out, successive governments have resisted calls to resentence those still on the jail term.

But a landmark ruling in the case of Leighton Williams, who served nearly 16 years over a drunken fight aged 19, has opened the floodgates. The appeal court ruled that a previous offence committed when he was 17 had been wrongly counted against him and his IPP sentence was quashed in 2024. Following his release, he told The Independent the unjust jail term had robbed him of 16 formative years.

Since then, a flurry of cases have been referred to the Court of Appeal and overturned, including that of Haroon Ahmed, who spent 18 years being punished for a knifepoint robbery of a service station committed when he was 19.

open image in gallery Haroon Ahmed’s IPP sentence was quashed after judges ruled it was not justified ( The Independent )

After it was quashed last year, he compared the plight of IPP prisoners to “hostages”, adding: “We have grown from teenagers to men, and we are watching people with much worse offending come to custody and be released.”

The CCRC now has a dedicated team examining applications from IPP and DPP prisoners. Recently, it referred its 11th case this year to the appeal courts.

Even with a streamlined process, progress is slow and revisiting every outstanding case would “take another CCRC”, Dame Vera admitted.

“The more we take notice of IPPs and the more we refer IPPs, the more IPPs we get sent in to us for review,” she said.

“I think really something far more wholesale needs to be done than this kind of pedalling along on a slow bicycle.”

In 2022, the cross-party justice committee inquiry found the sentences were “irredeemably flawed” and called for all IPP prisoners to be resentenced. Lord Thomas has also taken up the issue, urging parliamentarians to give prisoners a release date in a major report produced with the Howard League for Penal Reform.

And in a damning statement last month, the UN condemned the detention of UK prisoners trapped on IPP terms as “arbitrary” and accused the British government of presiding over a form of psychological torture.

In a scathing 16-page document, the Human Rights Council’s Working Group on Arbitrary Detention said the sentences amounted to “inhumane treatment” due to the “mental anguish of being subjected to continuous uncertainty of a release date”.

Dame Vera, a former victims’ commissioner, said she was not surprised the UN was looking at the scandal, adding it was time for each case to be reviewed “systematically and individually” while ensuring the public is protected.

“Literally, some of these guys don’t know they’re ever going to get out for what they did,” she said.

open image in gallery The newly appointed justice secretary Alex Norris has been urged to look at ending the scandal ( Getty )

“Fundamentally, the government accepted long ago that these were unwise sentences,” she added. “So, if the government has said these are bad sentences, surely it needs to devise a way of getting those who are left over off them.”

An Ungripp spokesperson welcomed Mr Burnham’s review but said they “have heard promises of action and reform before, only to see meaningful change delayed or fail to materialise”.

They called for an urgent resentencing exercise, adding: “The government cannot continue to outsource its moral responsibility to an under-resourced court system. We need urgent, state-led action through a proper resentencing exercise to finally give these written-off young adults their lives back.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “It is right that IPP sentences were abolished. The decision to quash individual sentences is a matter for the courts.

“While public protection is our number one priority, we are working with organisations and campaign groups to support those still serving these sentences, including through access to mental health support and rehabilitation programmes.”

More than half a month’s rainfall hit Scotland this weekend as England and Wales continued to brace for a fifth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures of 36C expected this week.

North-west Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland were in the path of heavy rain on Sunday, but the Met Office forecast the wet weather could move southwards, leaving cloud of Wales and central England overnight.

Meteorologist Tom Morgan said north-west Scotland had already seen over 100mm of rain on Friday and Saturday, while 19 counties across England saw 1mm or less throughout the whole of July.

Forecasters expect that tomorrow will be slightly cooler, but heatwave conditions will likely return later in the week, peaking at 36C in parts of East Anglia and the South East by Thursday.

open image in gallery Rain in Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland on Sunday ( Met Office )

Highs of up to 30C are possible in parts of England and Wales by Tuesday, increasing to 32C and 34C respectively by Wednesday.

Mike Silverstone, deputy chief forecaster at the Met Office, said: “Temperatures will climb through the weekend and, more significantly, through much of next week. After a brief dip on Monday, high pressure will move across the UK before settling to the east, allowing a southerly flow to develop.

“A fairly widespread heatwave is likely across large parts of England and Wales, with hot conditions developing in places. The heat is expected to peak for much of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland on Wednesday.”

He added: “Humidity levels are also expected to increase through the week, which may make conditions feel more uncomfortable, particularly overnight.”

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued yellow heat health alerts for the East Midlands, West Midlands, South East, South West, East of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, and London.

The yellow heat health alerts are in place until 9pm on Tuesday, but may well be extended as the hot weather continues.

The extreme weather of summer 2026 has included two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

Two more heatwaves in July, the driest July in England and Wales since records began in 1836, have fuelled drought and wildfires.

open image in gallery Tourists walk on the parched earth and sun-damaged grass near Tower Bridge on Sunday ( Getty )

Half of England and all of Wales were plunged into drought as the heatwaves gripped last month.

The UK’s health watchdog this week issued a warning to take extra precautions if people are taking medicine in the hot weather.

The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) said on Friday that drugs like ibuprofen and naproxen could increase sensitivity to the sun, making burns more likely.

Other treatments that can increase sensitivity include antibiotics like doxycycline and tetracycline, acne treatments like isotretinoin and topical retinoids, and antifungal medicines such as voriconazole, they said.

open image in gallery A drone view shows parched parkland around the Clifton Observatory in Bristol on Sunday ( Reuters )

Dr Alison Cave, chief safety officer at the MHRA, said: “Some commonly used medicines can affect the body’s ability to stay hydrated, regulate temperature, or protect itself from sun exposure.

“Simple precautions can make a significant difference. Staying hydrated, avoiding the strongest sun during the middle of the day, and using protective clothing and sunscreen can all help reduce risk.”

Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan, insisting Israel will not withdraw until Hamas fully disarms.

The US president claimed last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, which both Israel and Hamas agreed to last year and which started with the ceasefire.

Trump said that Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before ‌carrying out the October ​7, 2023 ‌attack on Israel that ⁠triggered the Gaza ⁠war, had agreed to lay ‌down ​its weapons.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," he added.

The Israeli prime minister said he is now in discussions with US officials about how to go forward, deeming some ideas “acceptable” while some “are not”.

open image in gallery Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan ( Reuters )

Last month, Egypt, which is mediating negotiations between Israel and Hamas, said that both sides had agreed to a new 15-point roadmap and that a future meeting would be held in Cairo “to discuss implementation mechanisms”.

Trump had thanked Egypt, Qatar and Turkey for brokering the agreement and called the deal “historic”.

A senior Hamas negotiator said at the time that the group’s disarmament was conditional on Israel fulfilling its commitments under the agreement, including withdrawing from Gaza and allowing the establishment of a national committee and reconstruction efforts.

Senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad said: “The agreement contains a clear provision stating that Israel must commit to and implement its obligations. If Israel does not implement the agreement, neither will we.”

open image in gallery Gaza has been reduced to rubble after Israel’s relentless attacks of the strip ( Reuters )

Israel’s rejection of the plan is a further blow for Trump who announced his Gaza peace plan in September last year.

Just months away from Israeli elections, Netanyahu is considered unlikely to pull back from his hardline stance.

Last month, the Israeli prime minister told his cabinet that he would not agree to requests from the US to withdraw troops from locations in Syria, Lebanon, and Gaza, according to Channel 13.

Sources told the broadcaster that Netanyahu said he would “stand on my own two feet and resist” amid growing pressure from the Israeli far-right for the military campaign to continue.

What was in Trump's 15-point plan for peace in Gaza?

The deal included the total disarmament ‌of Hamas and other groups in Gaza as well as the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territory.

It also stipulated that Hamas and “other factions” agree that “all civilian governance and security functions in Gaza shall be handed over” to a new technocratic body set up to run the enclave.

With that, the technocratic body would take over responsibility for handling “internal security incidents”.

The 15-point plan also said that that process would be “linked” to an Israeli withdrawal “in phases”, towards a complete withdrawal from the Palestinian enclave. There was no mention of a reconstruction process.

open image in gallery The Israeli PM is unlikely to pull back from his hardline stance ahead of the country’s elections ( GPO )

Under the initial deal to end the war, Israel was supposed to pull back to a demarcation point termed the Yellow Line, separating 47 per cent of the land controlled by the Palestinians from the 53 per cent controlled by Israel. Israel was supposed to steadily withdraw from its position, but has instead increased its area of control to around two-thirds.

The Board of Peace on Monday had hailed a “constructive and detailed” meeting between Netanyahu, Israeli officials and Gaza envoy Nikolay Mladenov.

The Board noted that the full withdrawal of the Israeli military beyond the Yellow Line “will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators”.

Hamas rejected the word “disarmament” but has said it would hand over its weapons for storage under the control of a US-backed Palestinian administration after Israel halted operations and withdrew its forces in line with last year's ceasefire.

An economist took live television interruption to a new level on Saturday when an insect flew into his mouth during a CNN interview about the U.S. economy.

University of Michigan professor Justin Wolfers was analyzing labor market data with CNN anchor Omar Jimenez when Wolfers accidentally swallowed a fly mid-interview. He was describing the U.S. labor market as “The Little Engine That Could” and noted it was “not earning an A+ in anyone’s book, but it does seem remarkably resilient so far.”

He added, “But, all resilient until the day that we’re not,” before he suddenly began coughing and struggling to speak.

Jimenez attempted to keep the segment moving to give Wolfers a moment to recover, asking, “You know, I just wonder, like, as we look ahead, everyone is looking — maybe not everyone — but, folks like yourself are looking at the Fed and trying to figure out, okay, we have these economic indicators, maybe the job market is a little softer, but how do you think the Fed is going to read this, considering they didn’t hike interest rates at the last meeting?”

“Mate, I just swallowed a fly on live television!” Wolfers said after managing to clear his throat.

open image in gallery University of Michigan professor Justin Wolfers was analyzing labor market data with CNN anchor Omar Jimenez when Wolfers accidentally swallowed a fly mid-interview ( CNN )

“I was trying to keep talking while you were coughing, so you could figure it out,” Jimenez responded. “It’s all good!”

Wolfers, an Australian native, joked about the situation on air, claiming that “Aussies love eating flies!” before tying the mishap back to Federal Reserve monetary policy.

“It might actually be a metaphor, because the biggest thing going on at the Fed is Kevin Warsh feels like I do right now,” Wolfers said, pausing to cough. “Kevin Warsh doesn’t like talking about what’s going on, and it makes both of us a little harder to understand and a little harder to interpret. So, you can think of Kevin as having swallowed the fly as well. I might swallow a horse; that will get the fly as well.”

Following the broadcast, Wolfers addressed the incident on X.

“A fly just zipped into my mouth while gabbing on CNN,” Wolfers wrote. “Next question was about the Fed, so I did what Kevin Warsh won't — I swallowed hard and kept talking. I figure folks deserve some clarity about the economy.”

He added: “(Postscript: The fly is dead. And I'm no longer a vegetarian.)”

News.title: Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund LIVE: Gunners concede another three goals in Emirates Cup defeat
News.content:
Why Arsenal Want Bruno Guimaraes So Badly

Arsenal suffered a second consecutive pre-season defeat ahead of the start of their Premier League title defence as clinical Borussia Dortmund won the Emirates Cup with a 3-2 victory.

New signing Bruno Guimaraes was unveiled to the Arsenal fans before kick-off and there was a party atmosphere as the Gunners returned to the Emirates for the first time since lifting the Premier League title in May.

Captain Martin Odegaard returned for the first time since the World Cup and Gabrel Magalhaes started in defence, but sharp finishes from the visitors’ Samuele Inacio and Konstantinos Karetsas left Arsenal two goals down before half-time.

Arsenal were beaten 3-1 by Real Betis In Dublin on Wednesday and quickly found themselves trailing by the same scoreline when Joane Gadou bundled in from a corner moments after Ethan Nwaneri had pulled one back.

Viktor Gyokeres gave Arsenal some late hope from the penalty spot before Arteta made further changes, introducing several players from the club’s academy. Gabriel Martinelli had the ball in the net in stoppage time but was given offside.

Arteta’s team will be back in action against Como on Wednesday, their final pre-season fixture before facing Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff next Sunday and Coventry City in their Premier League opener the following Friday.

News.content:

Andy Burnham has reportedly been presented with a new post-Brexit proposal which calls for Britain to rejoin the EU’s single market.

The proposal would see Britain promise to extend the protection of Britain’s Armed Forces and nuclear deterrent across Europe, in exchange for access to the EU’s free-trade zone.

The prime minister has promised to “consolidate the progress made on the existing UK-EU negotiations” undertaken by Sir Keir Starmer – but it is not yet known whether he will stick to his predecessor’s red lines as Labour draws up its manifesto for the next election, which included no return to freedom of movement and no return to the single market or customs union.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has said he will ‘consolidate’ progress made by his predecessor on the EU ( PA Wire )

According to The Telegraph, former Tory MP Nick Boles, who quit the party in 2019 over Brexit and went on to help Sir Keir prepare for government, has drawn up a plan which would allow Britain to rejoin the single market.

The proposal, which has reportedly been seen by top government officials, including national security adviser Jonathan Powell, is said to include the suggestion that Britain should push for the creation of a “European confederation”, which would link the single market with Nato’s defence commitments.

Ukraine, Switzerland, Norway and the Western Balkan countries would also be among those invited to join the confederation.

Britain’s obligations as part of the agreement would include spending 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence, and extending its nuclear umbrella across the non-Nato allies which Trident does not currently cover.

In exchange, the UK would be allowed to join the EU’s free trade zone without having to accept controversial terms, such as freedom of movement or having to join the Euro.

Europe: The Way Back We’re campaigning to rebuild Britain’s future in Europe JOIN US HERE

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Boles insisted a new strategy for defence cooperation with Europe is needed because there is no longer any guarantee Donald Trump will “defend Europe as if it were Kansas”.

“If we’re trying to do a bilateral negotiation in which we try to persuade the EU to have us have access to the single market for goods, we will fail,” he said.

“But if we make a proposal that solves other problems they have, like Ukraine… that’s the possibility where the selling might be easier. We can explain this isn’t just a selfish British deal, it’s a deal you can use to solve other problems yourselves.”

However, a Cabinet Office source pointed out that the government regularly receives “speculative policy ideas”, adding: “It would be incorrect to suggest these are all acted upon”.

It is understood the government is committed to the red lines set out in Sir Keir Starmer’s manifesto for the duration of this parliament.

Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock argued that Mr Boles’ plan is a “practical approach”, but warned that “the chances of such an advance are currently rather remote”.

The Labour peer told The Independent: “It’s a practical approach because it emphasises the mutual advantage of such an agreement and that is a crucial consideration.

“However, the chances of such an advance are currently rather remote, not least because of the necessarily strict adherence by the EU to the integrity of the Single Market.

“Participation is confined to member states and departure from that constitutional and practical provision would be unprecedented for any country outside the European Economic Area.”

He added: “The experience and losses of Brexit have radically reduced EU trust in the UK so any advances that will restore a relationship with the UK that is dependable and durable are difficult to achieve.”

But Liberal Democrat MP Al Pinkerton, the party’s Europe spokesperson, told The Independent that Andy Burnham should be “prepared to be ambitious about Europe”.

“Andy Burnham’s silence on Europe can’t last much longer”, he said. “If he wants to offer Labour and the country a different direction, he needs to tell us whether that includes dropping the government’s damaging red lines on Europe.

“Britain needs a government prepared to be ambitious about Europe. It’s time Andy Burnham told us whether he is,” he added.

Meanwhile, pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain said Mr Burnham’s “ambitious domestic agenda requires economic growth that can only be found by full EU membership, as our independent modelling by Frontier Economics shows”.

“While all creative ideas for closer relations with our nearest trading partner are welcome, the new prime minister is too patriotic to put Britain in a ‘rule-taker max’ position.

“Industry and voters want us to have an official seat at the table, to deliver for business, workers, the climate and urgently, the war against Putin,” Naomi Smith, the organisation’s chief executive said.

It comes just weeks after a government minister failed to rule out putting a promise to rejoin the EU in Labour’s next manifesto, suggesting that Mr Burnham could attempt to unpick Brexit in the next parliament.

Minister for European relations Hamish Falconer insisted that the government is “not talking about rejoining today”, but added: “What we do in our next manifesto will be a question for the Labour Party.”

The prime minister has previously said he is in favour of the UK rejoining the EU, but later clarified that he will not try to rejoin, arguing that the country would be stuck in a “permanent rut if we’re just constantly arguing”.

Asked last month how the new PM will approach Britain’s relationship with the EU, following a “reset” of relations undertaken by Sir Keir, Mr Falconer told Sky News: “The previous prime minister did really important work to help reset relations, and I want to consolidate some of that work. But we also need to see how we can go further.

“Even since we started those talks, the world has changed quite dramatically. The threats have changed quite dramatically – both talking about some of the threats in Eastern Europe, but clearly there are economic security threats, disinformation threats too.”

open image in gallery Nick Boles left the Tories and helped Sir Keir Starmer prepare for government ( PA )

Asked whether he agrees with former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, who called for Britain to rejoin the EU in a recent interview with The Independent, Mr Falconer said: “Look, the questions for the next manifesto are not yet sorted, but I think it’s been absolutely clear from what the prime minister has said, and I share his views on this: we had this vote 10 years ago. It was the will of the country. It was the will of my own constituency as well. We’re not backsliding from that.

“The world has changed since 2016. We need to make sure that our relationship with Europe changes too. Europe and the UK both face real challenges.”

Asked whether he could rule out reopening the issue of Brexit, he said: “We’re not talking about rejoining today. What we do in our next manifesto will also be a question for the Labour Party.”

Downing Street has been contacted for comment.

Andoni Iraola‘s first Anfield outing ended in defeat as Liverpool succumbed to back-to-back second-half capitulations in pre-season, losing late on to Monaco.

News.content:

On hot summer days, few things are more refreshing than a dip in the pool. But have you ever wondered if the pool is as clean as that crystal blue water appears?

As an immunologist and infectious disease specialist, I study how germs spread in public spaces and how to prevent the spread. I even teach a course called “The Infections of Leisure” where we explore the risks tied to recreational activities and discuss precautions, while also taking care not to turn students into germophobes.

Swimming, especially in public pools and water parks, comes with its own unique set of risks — from minor skin irritations to gastrointestinal infections. But swimming also has a plethora of physical, social and mental health benefits. With some knowledge and a little vigilance, you can enjoy the water without worrying about what might be lurking beneath the surface.

The reality of pool germs

Summer news headlines and social media posts often spotlight the “ick-factor” of communal swimming spaces. These concerns do have some merit.

open image in gallery Chlorine, which is widely used in pools, is effective at killing many pathogens ( Getty/iStock )

The good news is that chlorine, which is widely used in pools, is effective at killing many pathogens. The not-so-good news is that chlorine does not work instantly – and it doesn’t kill everything.

Every summer, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issues alerts about swimming-related outbreaks of illness caused by exposure to germs in public pools and water parks. A 2023 CDC report tracked over 200 pool-associated outbreaks from 2015 to 2019 across the U.S., affecting more than 3,600 people. These outbreaks included skin infections, respiratory issues, ear infections and gastrointestinal distress. Many of the outcomes from such infections are mild, but some can be serious.

Germs and disinfectants

Even in a pool that’s properly treated with chlorine, some pathogens can linger for minutes to days. One of the most common culprits is Cryptosporidium, a microscopic germ that causes watery diarrhoea. This single-celled parasite has a tough outer shell that allows it to survive in chlorine-treated water for up to 10 days. It spreads when faecal matter — often from someone with diarrhoea — enters the water and is swallowed by another swimmer. Even a tiny amount, invisible to the eye, can infect dozens of people.

Another common germ is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that causes hot tub rash and swimmer’s ear.

About the author Lisa Cuchara is a Professor of Biomedical Sciences at Quinnipiac University. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Viruses like norovirus and adenovirus can also linger in pool water and cause illness.

Swimmers introduce a range of bodily residues to the water, including sweat, urine, oils and skin cells. These substances, especially sweat and urine, interact with chlorine to form chemical byproducts called chloramines that may pose health risks.

These byproducts are responsible for that strong chlorine smell. A clean pool should actually lack a strong chlorine odour, as well as any other smells, of course. It is a common myth that a strong chlorine smell is a good sign of a clean pool. In fact, it may actually be a red flag that means the opposite – that the water is contaminated and should perhaps be avoided.

How to play it safe at a public pool

Most pool-related risks can be reduced with simple precautions by both the pool staff and swimmers. And while most pool-related illnesses won’t kill you, no one wants to spend their vacation or a week of beautiful summer days in the bathroom.

open image in gallery Most pool-related risks can be reduced with simple precautions ( Getty/iStock )
