In Mombasa County, the nurses strike paralysed medical services at all medical facilities, including Coast General Hospital, Port Reitz Hospital, Likoni District Hospital and Shimo La Tewa GK Prison Hospital.

Mombasa County, through its Counsel Murtaza Tajbhai, said that the strike had turned from a labour disagreement to a matter of immense public interest.

Tajbhai said that the nurses’ union proceeded with the said strike despite the Mombasa Public Service Board inviting the KNUNM officials for talks to avert the said strike.

The union had raised concerns over the 2025-2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), implementation of the 2017 Return to Work Formula and pension terms for Universal Health Coverage staff care guidelines for nurses and the reinstatement of 46 nurses dismissed in Kisii County.

However, in their petition, Mombasa County said that the said grievances could not be addressed by each county individually.

Mombasa County Service Board Chief Executive Officer Fadhil Maamum told the court in his affidavit that most of the demands required consultation with national institutions like the Salaries and Remuneration Commission, while others cannot be implemented immediately given their significant financial implications.

He said that nurses under Mombasa County have no salary arrears and had met some of the union’s demands through negotiations.

Maamum said that while the nurses’ grievances can be resolved, the patients do not have the luxury of time.

“Nurses are designated essential service providers under the Labour Relations Act and the industrial action was unlawful because the statutory dispute resolution mechanism had not been exhausted," said Maamum.

He said the court's intervention will allow for negotiations and safeguard the constitutional right to healthcare.

However, the Union said that the strike was after failed action by the counties to meet their agreed grievances despite continued negotiations.

The nurses said they will not be reporting to work unless guided by the union.

World.title: NTSA blamed for poor signage, costly penalties
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A temporary speed signage on Likoni Road, Nairobi. [Screengrab]

A growing number of motorists are raising concerns about fines issued by the National Transport and Safety Authority's (NTSA) automated speed camera system, claiming they are being penalised without sufficient warning, transparency, or an opportunity to challenge the alleged offences.

The complaints come after the government rolled out a nationwide network of smart traffic cameras aimed at curbing speeding and reducing road carnage.

The cameras automatically detect speeding vehicles, identify registration numbers and generate instant penalties, with notifications sent to registered vehicle owners via SMS.

While authorities have hailed the technology as a game-changer in road safety, many drivers say the system has become a source of frustration and financial burden.

Some motorists claim they have received multiple speeding fines within a single journey, while others argue they were penalised despite maintaining the posted speed limits.

In some places, motorists argue that most signs are on one side of the road, even though the road is a dual carriageway, making it difficult for most road users.

Several have questioned the accuracy of the cameras, citing cases where they were allegedly fined long after travelling through the affected roads.

The debate has been raging on social media, with the latest complaint being on the speed signage along Likoni Road, Nairobi, where motorists are mandated to drive at 30km/h.

"NTSA can't be the complainant, regulator, enforcer, prosecutor, Jury, judge, and collector all-in-one. They could be chasing internal collection targets, while hurting the common man,"

Others have expressed concern over the placement of some speed cameras, saying they are positioned in areas where speed limit signs are either unclear, obscured or insufficient.

"They fined me near Industrial Park Eastern Bypass where on that entire stretch there is no sign indicating the speed limit. This is a shakedown; someone is minting this money," a user on X lamented.

According to the drivers, this leaves road users vulnerable to inadvertent violations.

"There is no problem with enforcing traffic laws, but motorists deserve clear signage, accurate records and a fair opportunity to dispute fines they believe were issued in error," said one driver who recently received multiple speed notifications along the Northern Bypass.

The automated enforcement system forms part of NTSA's broader road safety reforms under the Minor Traffic Offences Framework, which allows specified offences to be handled administratively instead of through the courts.

NTSA says the initiative is intended to eliminate corruption associated with roadside enforcement, improve compliance with traffic laws and reduce the backlog of traffic cases in courts.

Under the framework, speeding attracts graduated penalties depending on how far a driver exceeds the prescribed limit.

Minor violations may attract warnings or lower fines, while more serious offences carry significantly higher penalties.

The automated fines programme also faced an earlier legal challenge after petitioners argued that motorists were being punished without adequate due process.

The dispute centred on whether automated enforcement infringed constitutional rights to fair administrative action and a fair hearing before penalties are imposed.

Road safety experts, however, maintain that excessive speed remains one of the leading causes of fatal crashes in Kenya and argue that consistent, technology-driven enforcement is more effective than sporadic roadside operations.

They contend that unlike manual enforcement, automated cameras minimise opportunities for bribery and apply traffic laws uniformly to all motorists.

Even so, transport stakeholders are urging NTSA to improve public awareness, ensure speed limit signs are visible and regularly calibrated, and establish an efficient appeals mechanism for motorists who believe they have been wrongly fined.

According to Volume 6 on Traffic Control Facilities and the Traffic Signs Manual, the Ministry of Transport is mandated to ensure the speed limit sign boards are erected above pedestrian footways with a minimum clearance of 2.2m from the bottom of the sign to the pavement.

At the same time, the signs should be placed at an absolute minimum horizontal clearance of 0.5 m from the outer edge of the usable shoulder or carriageway.

World.title: Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arraigned over alleged inciting remarks
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arrives at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi on August 4, 2026. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia was on Tuesday arraigned before the Milimani Law Courts over alleged inciting remarks made during a political rally in Kieni, Nyeri County.

Appearing before Senior Principal Magistrate Teresia Nyangena, Kaguchia was read the charge of offensive conduct by the court clerk but did not respond after his lawyers mounted a spirited constitutional challenge against the charges.

His legal team objected to the manner in which the charges had been framed, arguing they violated several constitutional safeguards and should not proceed.

The courtroom was packed to capacity as a battery of lawyers appeared for the legislator alongside political allies who turned up in solidarity.

Among those present were Nyeri Senator John Methu, Nyeri Woman Representative Jane Njeri Maina and several elected leaders who followed the proceedings from the public gallery.

The defence argued that the charge sheet failed to meet the constitutional threshold set under Article 50(2) which guarantees every accused person the right to be informed of the charge with sufficient detail to answer it.

The charge before you does not disclose an offence under the law and purely an attempt by the state to breach the freedom of expression and limiting the opposition.

Lead defence counsel Kiragu Wathuta and Ndegwa Njiru told the court that the MP's constitutional rights had been violated from the time of his arrest.

The lawyers narrated that on the night of August 2, Kaguchia had appeared on Inooro FM's Kiririmbi programme where public affairs were being discussed between 7 pm. and 9 pm.

According to the lawyer, after the programme ended, staff at the Royal Media Services station allegedly informed the MP that about 30 Subaru vehicles carrying hooded individuals had surrounded the premises looking for him.

"Because of the wave of abductions in this country, I advised him to remain within the Royal Media Services premises. At about 5 a.m., I found him having spent the night on the station's couches waiting for daylight," lawyer told the court.

He said that at around 9 a.m., a senior officer who identified himself as a regional DCI commander arrived with uniformed officers and informed the MP that he was under arrest despite there being no summons or warrant issued against him.

"When we inquired why no summons had been issued as is the normal procedure, the investigating officer told us they were acting on instructions from above," the lawuer submitted.

The lawyer further claimed officers initially indicated Kaguchia would be taken to Kilimani before driving him instead to DCI headquarters, where he said advocates were denied access to their client.

"They told us no counsel would be allowed into the DCI premises. Lawyers were locked out and denied an opportunity to consult with the accused," he said.

According to the defence, lawyers later moved to court and obtained orders from Kiambu High Court granting Kaguchia police bail of Sh100,000.

However, they alleged officers at Kamukunji Police Station refused to process the release despite the cash bail being available.

The lawyer told the court that the Officer Commanding Station allegedly declined to accept the money, saying he had received instructions that the legislator could not be released from the station and should instead deposit the cash bail at Central Police Station.

"The accused is not before this court because of any crime he committed. He is here to demonstrate to the country that it is now a crime to oppose the government," he argued.

Lawyer Wathuta also informed the court that Justice Gregory Mutai had on Tuesday morning in Milimani High Court Human Rights Petition No. E517 of 2026 granted the MP a bond of Sh500,000 and directed police to facilitate his access to legal counsel.

Lawyer Ndegwa Njiru argued that Kaguchia could not be required to plead before first receiving legal advice, citing Article 49(1)(c) of the Constitution, which guarantees every arrested person the right to communicate with and be represented by an advocate.

Njiru further challenged the jurisdiction of the Milimani court, arguing that the alleged offence was said to have occurred in Kieni, Nyeri County, and should therefore be prosecuted before a court with territorial jurisdiction over the alleged incident.

He also argued that the charge under Section 94(1) of the Penal Code was defective because it did not disclose who had allegedly been threatened, abused or insulted.

"The charge sheet merely refers to words allegedly uttered by the accused but fails to demonstrate that they were made in a public place or that they amounted to threatening, abusive or insulting words as required by law," Njiru submitted.

He also questioned the accuracy of the translated charge sheet, telling the court he understood Kikuyu and had noticed discrepancies between the original alleged utterances and the English translation.

Njiru argued that the translation distorted the alleged remarks, particularly the reference to the word "Kasongo", and maintained that the inconsistencies prejudiced the accused's ability to understand the charge.

He further submitted that the offence under Section 94 of the Penal Code is a misdemeanour punishable by a maximum sentence of six months imprisonment or a fine not exceeding Sh5,000.

Njiru argued that under Article 49(2) of the Constitution, Kaguchia ought not to have remained in custody for two nights over such an offence.

The defence also urged the court to order the release of the MP's Samsung A33 mobile phone, arguing that it had no connection to the alleged offence.

The hearing on the preliminary objections is still ongoing before Milimani Law Courts

World.title: Tension at Kamukunji Police Station as leaders demand Kaguchia's release
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukuruwe-ini MP John Kaguchia at Kamukunji Police Station in Nairobi on August 3, 2026. [Collins Oduor, Standard]

Tension is high at Kamukunji Police Station as opposition leaders led by Kipipiri MP Wanjiku Muhia and lawyers demand the immediate release of Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia, claiming police had failed to comply with a High Court order granting him police cash bail.

Kaguchia, who was arrested earlier on Monday over alleged electoral offences and incitement, remained in police custody hours after his lawyers said the court had ordered his release on Sh100,000 police bail.

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua in a post on his Facebook account said that the High Court had issued orders directing the Officer Commanding Station (OCS) at Kamukunji Police Station to release the legislator immediately upon payment of the bail.

Gachagua said that despite the court order having been served, the OCS had not acted and was instead awaiting instructions from his superiors. He warned the officer against disobeying a court order, saying that he could be held personally liable for contempt of court if the directive was ignored.

The former Deputy President further referenced the ongoing murder case involving the former OCS of Central Police Station, urging police officers to uphold the law and avoid carrying out unlawful instructions.

Several Members of Parliament from the Mt Kenya region have camped outside Kamukunji Police Station, insisting they would not leave until Kaguchia is released. The legislators accused police of delaying compliance with the court order and questioned why the MP was still being held despite the court's directive.

The lawmakers that claimed they had been redirected to Central Police Station while seeking information about Kaguchia's detention.

Kaguchia's arrest has sparked political debate, with opposition leaders accusing investigative agencies of selectively enforcing the law against government critics. They argue that other leaders who have previously made controversial public statements have not faced similar action.

World.title: AI isn’t the biggest cybersecurity problem. People are
World.content:
Cases of AI escaping the lab, infiltrating other companies and trying to deceive people have all made headlines in recent weeks. And in one case, AI models even worked together to break free from their test environments.

Does this mean the machines are taking over? Not quite.

AI isn’t the mastermind behind today’s most widespread cyber threats; it’s people who can use AI nefariously – and for nefarious purposes. AI has given bad actors massive power, allowing them to create malicious software, research targets, create convincing schemes and automate attacks at an unprecedented pace.

One in four data breaches were driven by AI from February 2025 to March 2026, according to an IBM report. And Americans lost more than $893 million to AI-related scams last year, the FBI says.

But experts say real-world threat actors – that is, people – are still the ones pulling the strings. AI agents have only perpetuated existing attack methods, like phishing and malware scams, rather than creating wholly new ones.

“It’s the humans that we need to watch out for,” said Oren Etzioni, professor emeritus at the University of Washington and former CEO of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence. “AI is just the tool.”

AI going rogue

Some recent incidents have shown what AI is capable of in the real world, not just in theory, igniting fears about whether the technology is advancing too quickly.

Those breaches also show how unpredictable AI can be when interpreting instructions. OpenAI’s models, for example, were trying to pass a cybersecurity test when they broke out of their test environment and breached another company, even though they weren’t told to do so.

Patrick Fussell, global head of adversary simulation at IBM, compared AI to a genie.

“You want to ask it a wish, but you have to be very, very specific about the details of your wish,” he told CNN. “Or it could sort of go awry.”

But these instances also happened under very specific circumstances.

OpenAI turned off restrictions that would have prevented its model from “pursuing high risk cyber activity.” Anthropic ran its tests without the standard safety safeguards in models that are generally available to the public. The AI Security Institute also turned off certain tools that could have “reduced the scope” of what the models were capable of.

Researchers typically do this to fully evaluate a model’s capabilities.

“I couldn’t go into ChatGPT or Claude or something like that, and it accidentally breaks into the FBI. That’s not going to happen,” said Adam Meyers, head of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. “So what we’re seeing is these are done in specific test conditions where they’re monitoring to see, ‘Does this thing do something that it’s not expected to do?”

How hackers are using AI

AI isn’t acting autonomously to come up with new attacks, experts say. Instead, it’s helping cyber criminals implement existing techniques much faster while being more efficient and effective.

That can include things like using AI to analyze a company’s website to figure out who to target or deploying an AI agent to handle initial negotiation talks with a cyber extortion victim. AI agents can mimic human conversations through both text and even specific voices. Hackers with little expertise can now leverage AI to pull off advanced schemes.

“They’re using (AI) to enhance the cyberattack methodology, essentially, in all the different stages, but it’s still kind of being run by the human,” said Jud Dressler, head of the risk operations center at cyber insurance firm Resilience.

Bad actors used to hastily scrap together basic scripts – instructions for automating tasks – to achieve their goals, according to Meyers. But now they’re able to churn out higher quality work that looks like it would have taken three times as long to produce.

They’re also using AI for behind-the-scenes work like generating the infrastructure needed to put up malicious websites.

“With AI, they could automate that buildout, and so the cost of rebuilding became very small and that changes the game,” said Rob Lefferts, corporate vice president of threat protection at Microsoft.

The bigger threat

For Etzioni, the recent incidents are a “canary in the coal mine” moment for AI and cybersecurity. And he’s not alone; Nobel prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, known popularly as the “godfather of AI,” recently warned that more rogue AI attacks are likely to come.

The rogue AI reports underscore the importance of implementing strong cybersecurity practices, such as patching vulnerabilities, monitoring AI agents in the workplace and being wary of social engineering and phishing scams, experts say.

But as advanced as AI is becoming, it’s still a program being orchestrated by a human. And those humans are the bigger concern because they’re the ones making the decisions, like conducting espionage or scamming users out of huge sums of cash, says Meyers.

Tech giants are racing to make AI as intelligent as humans, a theoretical milestone known as “artificial general intelligence.” The recent incidents, however, have heightened calls for a slowdown.

More than 1,200 workers at top AI companies, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, recently signed an open letter calling for the government to help pace AI development. The White House met with major AI companies last week to discuss a framework that would allow the government to review certain AI models before they’re released.

Cybersecurity researchers have likely considered the threats of AGI because those in the field tend to be paranoid, said IBM’s Fussell. But we’re still far from a reality in which AI agents are as smart as humans, he says.

“It’s like asking someone, ‘What would it be like to live on a different planet?’” he said. “You can sort of imagine, but it’s so beyond our ability to really make a plan for.”

World.title: How both Iran and Oman have economic claims to the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Iran is waiting for “final approval” on a proposed framework agreement with Oman for shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported yesterday.

Under the agreement, Iranian and Omani routes will remain in use temporarily before traffic is redirected through a central course, according to Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency. Officials in Iran would oversee inbound traffic, while their Omani counterparts would manage outbound traffic, Fars said.

The vital Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed by Iran since the US and Israel began the war back in February. It is the main route for shipping crude from oil-rich countries such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to the rest of the world.

Both Tehran and Muscat have Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) in the strait.

According to the United Nations, a state has “sovereign rights” to explore, exploit, conserve and manage the natural resources of the waters in its EEZ.

However, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), “ships of all States, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea.”

A coastal state should not “hamper the innocent passage of foreign ships through the territorial sea,” it says, except in specific outlined scenarios. It may “take the necessary steps in its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent,” UNCLOS outlines.

CNN’s Aida Karimi and Sana Noor Haq contributed to this reporting.

World.title: Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan, saying no withdrawal until Hamas disarms
World.content:
Israel has rejected the latest US plan to move towards the next stage of peace in Gaza, demanding the full disarmament of Hamas before any Israeli forces withdraw.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the beginning of a cabinet meeting Sunday.

He said the Israeli military would “not withdraw at all until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens.”

“And when I say disarm Hamas, that means heavy weapons, less-heavy weapons, all weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not a fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

“We are now discussing this with the Americans. They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.”

“As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will be established — not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” Netanyahu said.

At the end of July, US President Donald Trump announced what he described as a historic agreement to secure the disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza, months after the president first announced a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Hamas and Israel.

Hamas said it would only go through with the deal if Israel halts strikes in Gaza and pulls troops back to the “yellow line,” as defined by the October ceasefire agreement.

Israeli forces currently occupy more than half of Gaza, in the east and south of the territory.

World.title: UEFA confirms payout to ex-employee under Infantino, amid denials of an affair
World.content:
FIFA chief Gianni Infantino is denying a report that inappropriate conduct was behind a six-figure “departure payment” made to a woman during his years as general secretary at the Union of European Football Associations.

UEFA confirmed the woman’s payout, noting that while it was not out of line at the time, internal regulations have since been “tightened.”

The British newspaper The Telegraph first reported allegations that the woman was paid because of an affair with the beleaguered head of world football.

Infantino “strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue,” a FIFA spokesperson told The Telegraph.

“Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” the statement added. CNN has reached out to FIFA for comment.

Ever since Infantino and FIFA’s controversial plans to sell partial commercial and operational rights to the World Cup were leaked two weeks ago, soccer’s world governing body has come under immense pressure, even after those plans were scrapped.

UEFA, which counts some of the world’s most powerful soccer nations among its members, has threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and publicly declared its loss of confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

This latest chapter in soccer’s civil war was sparked when The Telegraph published an article Friday alleging that “UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Gianni Infantino while he was its general secretary.”

The paper, citing multiple anonymous sources, claimed that Infantino had a “relationship with a junior employee” during his tenure at the helm of UEFA from 2009 to 2016. She was promoted to a “more lucrative managerial role,” and received a “payment” when she left the organization, the paper reported. UEFA also paid for her MBA course, the report added. She was not named in the report.

In a statement to CNN, UEFA confirmed a “departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school.”

“The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time,” the organization added. “Such regulations have been tightened since 2016 and the current staff regulations – which apply to all UEFA employees at whatever level – reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organization.”

On Saturday, FIFA issued a statement condemning efforts to circumvent the organization’s “statutes, democratic procedures and established governance framework.”

“It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President,” FIFA’s statement said. “Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA’s established democratic processes.”

The statement went on to say, “FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, FIFA will challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Senior FIFA officials threw their support behind Infantino after a crisis meeting on Wednesday, but UEFA is still threatening to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups. It doubled down on the threat even after the sell-off plans were jettisoned, saying it needs assurances that nothing like this will happen again.

If that threat came to pass, it would hugely devalue any World Cup since six of the current top 10 teams in both men’s and women’s soccer would not compete in the tournament.

FIFPRO, the players’ union, has also said its confidence in FIFA’s leadership “has now been fundamentally broken.”

However, CONMEBOL, which oversees South American soccer and opposed the plans, has said it won’t back an extraordinary congress to vote on Infantino’s future and will follow the existing timeline for the presidential election, which is set for early next year.

The Confederation of African Football, which is more dependent on the money FIFA distributes than other continental confederations, has backed Infantino.

CNN’s Ben Church, Thomas Schlachter and Kevin Dotson contributed to this report.

World.title: Egypt condemns attack on UAE oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned the targeting of an oil tanker operated by Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) with a missile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, describing the incident as a serious threat to maritime security, navigation and freedom of trade through one of the world’s key waterways.

In a statement, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry expressed full solidarity with the UAE and firmly rejected acts targeting ships and civilian facilities or threatening maritime safety in the region.

Egypt stressed the need to respect freedom of navigation through international waterways and prevent any actions that could endanger it.

Cairo also renewed its call for de-escalation and urged all parties to prioritize political and diplomatic solutions to help safeguard regional security and stability.

World.title: Egypt, Iraq FMs discuss regional developments, efforts on de-escalation
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty held a phone call Saturday, August 8, 2026, with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein to discuss bilateral relations and regional developments.

The two ministers stressed the importance of building on the growing momentum in Egyptian-Iraqi ties, expanding cooperation across various fields and maintaining coordination on issues of mutual concern.

They exchanged views on developments in the region and future security arrangements, emphasizing the need for joint efforts to reduce tensions, prioritize dialogue and support political and diplomatic solutions to regional crises.

The ministers also underscored the importance of strengthening the trilateral cooperation mechanism between Egypt, Iraq and Jordan as a promising framework for regional integration and for increasing the three countries’ human and economic resources.

They stressed the need to build on the achievements made under the mechanism aimed at supporting the aspirations of the three peoples for greater development and shared prosperity.

World.title: Egypt uncovers ancient cemetery in Daqahliya
World.content:
An Egyptian archaeological mission has uncovered an ancient cemetery and settlement in Daqahliya Governorate, revealing evidence of human occupation in the eastern Nile Delta spanning thousands of years.

The Supreme Council of Antiquities said that excavations at the Kom el Khilgan archaeological site uncovered burials dating from the Predynastic Period through the Greek and Roman eras, as well as a settlement from the Second Intermediate Period.

The oldest finds date to the first half of the fourth millennium BC and include simple oval burial pits containing human remains, handmade pottery and seashells. The number of burials suggests that a sizeable community lived in the area at the time.

Archaeologists also discovered mud-brick buildings, grain silos, ovens and hearths dating from the Second Intermediate Period and continuing into the New Kingdom.

Tombs from the 15th to 17th Dynasties were also found, providing evidence that the area was inhabited during the Hyksos period, when nearby Avaris was their capital. Burial objects included jewelry, amulets, scarabs, bronze tools and weapons, and pottery.

Other discoveries included an early 18th Dynasty mud-brick tomb and Ptolemaic burials, including the remains of a child placed inside two reused amphorae.

Excavations are continuing at the site to uncover further evidence about settlement, daily life and burial practices in the eastern Nile Delta.

World.title: Egypt, Chad expand cooperation in civil aviation
World.content:
The Egyptian-Chadian Business Forum discussed opportunities to boost economic and investment cooperation and broaden partnership between the two countries, alongside specialized talks on civil aviation aimed at developing air connectivity and passenger and cargo transport between Egypt and Chad.

Discussions were held as part of the fourth session of the Egyptian-Chadian Joint Committee, convened in the Chadian capital, N’Djamena, with the participation of a number of ministers, officials, and business community representatives from both sides.

In line with the political leadership’s directives to strengthen Egypt’s relations with African countries and expand areas of cooperation and regional integration, and pursuant to a mandate from Civil Aviation Minister Sameh El-Hefny, Captain Sameh Mohamed Fawzy, head of the Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority (ECAA), and pilot Karim Gamil, adviser to the ECAA chairman and director general of agreements, joined the Egyptian delegation.

They held talks with the Chadian side on ways to develop cooperation in civil aviation and expand passenger and cargo traffic between the two countries.

Discussions included a meeting with Fatime Goukouni Weddeye, Chad’s Minister of Transport, Civil Aviation and National Meteorology, which addressed ways to facilitate operating procedures, overcome challenges facing airlines in both countries, and explore opportunities to increase air traffic between the two sides.

The Egyptian delegation also held talks with the head of the Chadian Civil Aviation Authority and the relevant working team on mechanisms to expand passenger and cargo operations and enhance direct coordination between the two civil aviation authorities to quickly address any operational obstacles.

Talks resulted in an agreement to increase the operational capacity allocated for passenger transport by 100 percent, effectively doubling it, as well as raising air cargo capacity by 125 percent. The measures are aimed at enabling air transport to keep pace with expected growth in travel and trade between the two countries.

The two sides also agreed to maintain technical and operational coordination, exchange expertise and provide technical support in areas of mutual interest in civil aviation, with the aim of enhancing operational efficiency and facilitating the work of airlines.

As part of efforts to support bilateral cooperation, the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on civil aviation, establishing frameworks for cooperation and expertise-sharing while supporting the development of the air transport system and expanding cooperation between institutions and companies operating in the aviation sector in both countries.

These steps underscore the importance of civil aviation as a pillar of regional integration by expanding connectivity networks, facilitating the movement of people and goods, linking markets, and promoting trade and investment. They are also expected to support the shared interests of Egypt and Chad and advance development and integration efforts across Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Suspended Monrovia Central Prison Deputy Superintendent Alleges Irregular Arrest, Names Officials in Public Statement Tied to Drug Case
World.content:
Jackson K. Kolako says he was detained for six days after resisting an unlogged, after-hours visit to an inmate linked to Liberia’s multi-million-dollar narcotics case

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — Jackson K. Kolako, Deputy Superintendent for Operations at the Monrovia Central Prison (MCP), has gone public with a detailed account of his August 1 arrest, alleging he was detained for nearly a week and pressured to surrender his phones and passwords after he tried to enforce standard visitation procedures during an unannounced visit to an inmate connected to Liberia’s ongoing multi-million-dollar drug case.

Kolako’s account, posted publicly and addressed to several Liberian media outlets and journalists, has not been independently verified by FrontPageAfrica. It represents his version of events. FrontPageAfrica has reached out to the officials named in the statement for comment and will update this story with any response.

What Kolako says happened

According to his statement, the episode began around 1:30 p.m. on August 1, when two individuals identifying themselves as National Security Agency (NSA) agents arrived at MCP wearing shorts — attire he says is prohibited inside the facility — and declined to log their names or purpose in the visitor book, citing a “covert” mission to interview an inmate tied to the drug case.

Kolako says that while prison staff worked to verify the visitors’ identities, two senior corrections officials not assigned to MCP arrived and overrode standard entry procedures, with one allegedly declaring, “We make the law, and we can break the law.”

He says he asked whether the MCP’s Chief Superintendent and the Assistant Minister for Corrections had been notified, was told they had not, and was informed the visit was authorized above the Ministry of Justice’s Corrections Department. Kolako says he then called both officials — Chief Superintendent Colonel Roosevelt Varney and Assistant Minister Gabriel Fayiah Ndupellar — who told him they had no prior knowledge of the visit.

Kolako says he ordered the inmate in question, who had been outside for exercise, back to his housing unit, and resumed his regular duties overseeing roughly 1,800 inmates and nearly 100 officers.

The arrest

Kolako alleges that Siafa Bahn Kemokai then arrived at MCP with several Liberia National Police (LNP) officers and ordered his arrest — in what Kolako describes as a calculated attempt to provoke prison officers into resisting, which he feared could have triggered unrest that inmates might exploit to attempt an escape. He says he left the scene without incident to avoid his officers witnessing the arrest.

He says he was taken to LNP headquarters, where he was held from August 1 to August 7 without a formal statement being taken. On August 3, he alleges he was compelled — in the presence of senior Ministry of Justice prison officials, NSA agents, and LNP’s Unit 105 — to have his mobile phones brought in and to surrender his passwords. That evening, he says he was accused of cartel membership and of receiving payments from drug traffickers, allegations he denies.

Kolako says he refused an instruction to go home that night, choosing to remain in custody until he felt his safety was assured, and used the time to alert coworkers and family to his situation. He says he was released on August 7 and handed a suspension letter alleging he had disrupted an inmate interview involving an external security agency — a charge he disputes, noting he does not drink or smoke and questioning why he was referred to LNP custody rather than the Ministry of Justice’s internal disciplinary board.

His background and appeal

In his statement, Kolako describes twelve years in law enforcement following nine years as a classroom teacher and three as a National Transit Authority conductor, saying his net monthly salary never exceeded US$224 and that he has maintained what he calls an unblemished record.

He named four individuals he asked the public to keep in mind as the matter is investigated: Siafa Bahn Kemokai, Lawrence G. Bohlen, Samuel Lance Jasper, and Raymond A. Messan.

Kolako closed his statement with an appeal to Attorney General and Minister of Justice Cllr. Oswald N. Tweh, NSA head Rt. Gen. Prince C. Johnson, Minister of National Defense Rt. Gen. Geraldine Janet George Johnson, LNP head Col. Gregory O. Coleman, Sarah Beslow Nyanti, and the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia, asking that detainees held in connection with the multi-million-dollar drug case be moved to a secure holding facility abroad — he suggested Morocco — pending trial, to avoid undermining the Boakai administration’s anti-drug campaign.

Context

Kolako’s statement surfaces amid a broader shake-up tied to Liberia’s cocaine trafficking scandal, which has already led to the dismissal of several officials, including a former Roberts International Airport deputy and, separately, two immigration officers allegedly caught with narcotics crossing from Sierra Leone in March. It also comes as the government pursues the IB Atlantic IV, a cargo vessel suspected of links to the same drug case, which was recently arrested in Ivory Coast.

FrontPageAfrica has not confirmed the identities or roles of the individuals named in Kolako’s account beyond what is stated in his own statement, and could not independently verify claims regarding the inmate visit, the arrest, or the conditions of his detention. This newspaper has sought comment from the Ministry of Justice, the National Security Agency, and the Liberia National Police, and will update this story as responses are received.

World.title: Liberia: IB Atlantic IV Seized in Ivory Coast, Liberia Moves to Bring Vessel Home
World.content:
Ivorian authorities take control of the ship that eluded Liberian pursuit for weeks; Coast Guard seeks Sea Shepherd escort as questions over cargo remain unanswered

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia — The cargo vessel at the center of Liberia’s widening drug-trafficking scandal, the IB Atlantic IV, has been arrested in Ivory Coast and is now in the custody of Ivorian security authorities, bringing a dramatic turn to a chase that has consumed the country’s maritime agencies for more than a week.

The Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) has notified the National Security Agency and the Armed Forces of Liberia of the development, and officials are now working to secure a Sea Shepherd Global vessel to escort the ship back to Liberian waters, according to sources familiar with the operation. The IB Atlantic IV is currently docked at a port in Ivory Coast.

It remains unclear whether any narcotics were found aboard the vessel.

A chase that spanned three countries

Liberia had earlier alerted both Ivory Coast and Guinea that the vessel was at sea, part of a broader regional appeal for help tracking a ship that Liberian Coast Guard vessels — under-resourced for long-distance pursuit — had been unable to intercept on their own.

The request for regional assistance capped weeks of confusion and institutional finger-pointing that FrontPageAfrica has chronicled in detail since the vessel first surfaced in Liberian waters.

How the story unfolded

The IB Atlantic IV first drew scrutiny in early August, when it was spotted drifting near York Island in the Tewor District of Grand Cape Mount County. Security agencies — the Coast Guard, the National Security Agency, and the Armed Forces — struggled to establish contact, and each pointed to the other when FrontPageAfrica asked who was actually in charge of the response.

A 41-year-old general cargo ship flagged in Comoros — a registry shipping analysts regard as offering minimal oversight — the vessel’s own tracking data told a story that didn’t match the government’s. While a government source described a ship in distress off Sierra Leone, supposedly bound for Guinea-Bissau, the ship’s transponder placed it in West African waters barely moving, with a declared destination of Lomé, Togo.

Adding to the intrigue, FrontPageAfrica reported that authorities were examining claims that a smaller boat approached the vessel at sea in the days after it was first spotted, and appeared to attempt to pass something aboard — a detail that, if confirmed, would suggest the “distressed” ship was in fact waiting at a fixed position for a delivery.

The airport official’s letter

The controversy deepened with the emergence of a July 13 letter written by Mark Egon Kuiah, then a deputy at Roberts International Airport, who signed the correspondence not in his government role but as registered agent for a company called Madris Group of Companies Incorporated. The letter asked the Liberia Maritime Authority to grant the vessel docking rights and a dive team at the Freeport of Monrovia, describing it as disabled and in distress.

LiMA rejected the request, telling FrontPageAfrica the account didn’t hold up — the ship had not docked anywhere and was still in Sierra Leonean waters, yet was already being sought a Liberian berth. Kuiah was dismissed from his airport post weeks later, part of a broader shake-up tied to Liberia’s cocaine scandal that has also implicated the former commander of the Liberia Immigration Service post at Bo-Waterside and his deputy, both allegedly detained in Sierra Leone in March while carrying suspected narcotics back into Liberia.

The pursuit off Rivercess

Once the vessel drifted onto the Liberian side of the maritime border, authorities issued a search-and-seizure order. What followed, in the words of one official, became less an operation than a pursuit — Liberia’s Coast Guard, lacking vessels built for long-range chases, trailed the ship off Rivercess as it kept moving, aided in tracking efforts by Nigerian partners.

A system under scrutiny

The episode has already reshaped debate in Monrovia well beyond the ship itself. FrontPageAfrica’s editorial board has argued the IB Atlantic IV saga exposed a government that struggled for the better part of a week to tell the public what was moving through its own waters — even as lawmakers press ahead with a bill to split port oversight among four separate authorities. Critics say the case argues against decentralization, not for it, until the country can show it has the capacity to act quickly against a single threat, let alone four.

The scandal has also renewed pressure on the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, which has cycled through leadership shake-ups over the past year, and prompted the Senate’s National Security Committee to vow it will not be swayed by political pressure in confirming the agency’s next leadership.

What’s next

With the vessel now in Ivorian hands, attention turns to whether Liberian authorities will be granted access to search the ship, what if anything is found aboard, and how quickly the government can execute the handover it is now trying to arrange. FrontPageAfrica will continue to update this developing story.

This story is developing. Additional details will be added as they become available.

World.title: Liberia: Dismissed LNP Commander Seeks Bail In Liberia’s Biggest Cocaine Case
World.content:
Former Highway Patrol Chief Wadell W. Kwabo Challenges Detention as Court Battle Intensifies in US$317 Million Drug Trafficking Scandal

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-Former Liberia National Police Highway Patrol Commander Wadell W. Kwabo, one of the highest-ranking security officials to be criminally charged in Liberia’s largest cocaine trafficking investigation, has formally petitioned Criminal Court “C” at the Temple of Justice for bail, arguing that prosecutors have failed to establish sufficient evidence linking him to the multi-million-dollar drug trafficking operation that has shaken the country’s security establishment.

Kwabo, who was dismissed from the Liberia National Police by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai following the findings of a Joint National Security Investigative Task Force, is accused of using official police resources to facilitate the movement of an estimated 4.2 metric tons of cocaine valued at approximately US$317 million.

The case has become one of the most consequential anti-narcotics prosecutions in Liberia’s history, exposing alleged collusion between transnational drug traffickers and senior state security personnel.

Through his lawyers, headed by Cllr. Sayma Syrnius Cephus, Kwabo contends that “proof is not evident and presumption is not great” to justify his continued detention.

The defense argued that prosecutors have failed to produce objective evidence placing him at the crime scene before or during the commission of the alleged offenses and insists that the accusations against him rest primarily on statements made by co-defendant Christian Nyantee, who is allegedly attempting to reduce his own criminal liability by implicating others.

According to the defense motion, Kwabo is being prosecuted largely because investigators alleged that he provided an escort to the principal defendants after the crimes had already been committed.

His lawyers maintained that providing security escort is a routine responsibility of the Highway Patrol Section, particularly during operations involving members of Liberia’s national security apparatus. They insisted that there is no evidence proving he had prior knowledge that narcotics were being transported.

How Kwabo Became Entangled

Kwabo’s legal troubles emerged from an extensive investigation launched jointly by the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency and the Liberia National Police following the discovery of what authorities described as Liberia’s largest cocaine trafficking network.

Inspector General of Police Gregory O. W. Coleman disclosed during the investigation that security personnel were allegedly recruited to facilitate the movement of the narcotics from a coastal landing site to a secure holding location.

Investigators concluded that marked Liberia National Police patrol vehicles were allegedly deployed in a two-vehicle escort formation, with one police unit leading and another trailing the convoy transporting the cocaine.

Authorities alleged that Kwabo, then serving as Chief of the Highway Patrol Section, played a central role in coordinating or facilitating that police escort.

The investigation further revealed that the cocaine shipment allegedly entered Liberia through a sophisticated transnational trafficking network involving foreign nationals, including a Serbian national, who investigators say exploited private airstrips and coastal landing points before moving the drugs inland with assistance from local collaborators.

Based on the findings of the Joint National Security Investigative Task Force, Kwabo was arrested, formally charged, and forwarded to court together with Anthony T. Blaye, then Chief of the LNP Financial Crime Division.

Investigators alleged that both officers abused their official positions to protect one of the largest illicit drug shipments ever intercepted in Liberia.

Historic Drug Bust

The investigation represents an unprecedented chapter in Liberia’s anti-drug campaign.

Unlike previous narcotics cases in which public officials were accused of negligence or failure to act, investigators alleged that serving senior police commanders physically participated in transporting cartel drugs using official government vehicles.

Investigators described the operation as highly organized, involving international traffickers, local collaborators, airport-linked operatives, and security personnel.

On July 30, Liberian authorities publicly destroyed approximately 4.2 metric tons of seized cocaine, valued at nearly US$317 million, during what officials described as the country’s largest drug destruction exercise.

The public incineration was intended to demonstrate Liberia’s renewed commitment to dismantling international narcotics networks and to signal that the country would no longer serve as a safe transit point for organized drug trafficking.

Presidential Action

Following the submission of the Joint National Security Investigative Task Force report, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai ordered sweeping disciplinary measures against officials implicated in the investigation.

Among those dismissed were Former Highway Patrol Chief Wadell W. Kwabo, Former Financial Crime Division Chief Anthony T. Blay, and

Several other security and airport officials identified by investigators as having allegedly played various roles in facilitating or failing to prevent the movement of the narcotics.

The President also directed that all individuals identified by investigators be turned over to the appropriate prosecutorial authorities for criminal proceedings. At the same time, additional investigations continued into possible wider networks operating within Liberia’s security institutions and airport system.

The dismissals marked one of the largest disciplinary actions ever taken against serving security personnel over alleged drug trafficking.

Investigation Widens

The investigation has continued to expand beyond the initial arrests.

In recent developments, investigators arrested Moses Jallah, an officer of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, who is now under investigation for his alleged connection to aspects of the wider narcotics network.

Security has also arrested a prominent private bar owner, George Leroy Henries, who investigators believe may possess information relevant to the movement of suspects and the broader trafficking enterprise.

Both individuals remained under investigation as authorities seek to identify additional local collaborators and determine the full scope of the international criminal network.

Investigators have repeatedly indicated that further arrests remain possible as forensic examinations, financial investigations, telecommunications analyses, and intelligence gathering continue.

Defense Challenges Evidence

However, Kwabo’s lawyers argued that prosecutors have failed to satisfy the constitutional standard required to deny bail.

The motion maintained that no independent evidence connects Kwabo to planning or participating in the alleged conspiracy and argues that the prosecution relies almost exclusively on the statements of an alleged accomplice whose testimony has not been independently corroborated.

The defense further contends that Liberian law requires more than suspicion or association before an accused person may be denied liberty pending trial.

Counsel insists that the prosecution has failed to establish reasonable grounds demonstrating that Kwabo knowingly participated in the trafficking operation or intentionally assisted the principal defendants.

The motion, therefore, requests the court to admit him to bail while awaiting trial.

Case Still Unfolding

Criminal Court “C” has yet to rule on the bail application.

Meanwhile, prosecutors continue building what has become one of the largest organized crime prosecutions in Liberia’s recent history.

With multiple defendants already before the court, additional suspects under active investigation, and security agencies pledging to dismantle every level of the alleged trafficking network, the case continues to expose what investigators believe was a deeply coordinated operation involving international drug traffickers and local collaborators embedded within key state institutions.

The outcome of the prosecution is expected to test the country’s criminal justice system and its resolve to combat transnational organized crime while determining whether senior public officials entrusted with enforcing the law instead became facilitators of one of the country’s largest cocaine trafficking operations.

World.title: Liberia: LDEA OIC Denies Receiving Toyota Pickup From Man Charged in $317M Cocaine Case, Welcomes Independent Probe
World.content:
Monrovia – The Officer-in-Charge of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA), Deputy Commissioner of Police Fitzgerald T. M. Biago, has strongly rejected allegations linking him to individuals accused in Liberia’s multimillion-dollar cocaine trafficking investigation, insisting that he has never accepted gifts, favors or benefits in exchange for compromising his official duties.

By Edwin G. Genoway Jr.

Biago’s denial follows allegations by political activist Martin K. N. Kollie, who claimed in a lengthy social media post that the LDEA chief received a Toyota Hilux pickup truck from George Harris, also known as Leroy Harris, a man reportedly charged by Liberian authorities in connection with the country’s US$317 million cocaine seizure.

Biago dismissed the allegations as false and misleading, saying they are not supported by credible evidence.

“I categorically reject these allegations as false, misleading, and without credible evidence,” Biago stated in a Facebook post.

The LDEA chief said his career has been dedicated to serving Liberia, upholding the law and carrying out his responsibilities with professionalism and integrity.

“I have never accepted any gift, favor, or benefit from any individual or criminal organization in exchange for compromising my duties,” he asserted.

Kollie Questions Toyota Hilux

At the center of Kollie’s allegations is a grey Toyota Hilux pickup truck that he claims is being used by Biago.

Kollie alleged that vehicle registration information he obtained lists George Wha Harris as the registered owner of the pickup, bearing license plate A532084.

According to Kollie, the vehicle was entered into the registration system in November 2024 and registered under Harris’ name. He used the alleged registration information to question how the vehicle came into Biago’s possession and whether it was provided to the LDEA chief by Harris.

However, registration of a vehicle in an individual’s name does not, by itself, establish that the vehicle was subsequently given to another person as a gift or benefit. That claim would require independent verification.

Kollie also alleged that another vehicle was purchased for Biago’s wife by individuals linked to the alleged narcotics network, but the claim was not independently substantiated in the material he published.

Claims of Security Links

Beyond the vehicle allegation, Kollie claimed that Harris maintained relationships with senior security officials, including Biago.

He further alleged that individuals involved in narcotics trafficking had developed relationships within Liberia’s security institutions, particularly the LDEA and the Liberia National Police.

Kollie called for Biago’s resignation or dismissal and urged that the allegations be subjected to a formal investigation.

He also indicated that he intends to release additional information concerning what he described as an alleged drug trafficking network and its suspected collaborators.

Biago Welcomes Investigation

Despite rejecting the allegations, Biago said he is prepared to cooperate with any legitimate investigation by the appropriate authorities.

He stressed, however, that any investigation must be independent, impartial and grounded in evidence rather than social media claims and speculation.

“I remain fully prepared to cooperate with any lawful, independent, and impartial investigation, as I am confident that the truth will prevail through due process rather than speculation or misinformation,” Biago wrote.

His response comes amid heightened public scrutiny of Liberia’s national drug enforcement efforts following major cocaine seizures and ongoing investigations into alleged narcotics trafficking networks.

‘My Focus Remains on the Drug Fight’

Biago said the allegations would not distract him from his responsibilities as head of the LDEA.

He reaffirmed his commitment to combating illicit drug trafficking, dismantling criminal networks and apprehending individuals involved in narcotics-related activities.

“My focus remains steadfast on leading the fight against illicit drugs and dismantling these networks,” he said.

The LDEA has similarly rejected claims that Biago received a vehicle from an alleged drug trafficker, describing the allegation as unsupported by any credible record, documentation or verifiable evidence.

The Agency has encouraged anyone with credible evidence of misconduct to submit it to the appropriate investigative authorities for independent and lawful review.

Allegations Require Verification

The allegations against Biago remain unproven and should not be treated as established facts unless substantiated through an official investigation or judicial proceedings.

The claims presented by Kollie, including the alleged vehicle transfer, do not by themselves establish that Biago participated in drug trafficking, accepted a bribe or committed any criminal offense.

Biago has denied the allegations and has expressly indicated his willingness to face a lawful and independent investigation.

The broader narcotics investigation also remains subject to due process, with individuals accused or charged in connection with the cocaine case entitled to the presumption of innocence unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

For Biago, however, the message is clear: he says the allegations will not deter him from leading Liberia’s fight against illicit drugs.

“My focus remains steadfast on leading the fight against illicit drugs and dismantling these networks,” he said.

World.title: Liberia: LDEA Dismisses Claims OIC Biago Received Pickup From Alleged Drug Trafficker
World.content:
Monrovia – The Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) has rejected allegations that its Officer-in-Charge, Deputy Commissioner of Police Fitzgerald T. M. Biago received a Toyota pickup truck from an individual allegedly linked to drug trafficking.

The allegations were made by political activist Martin K. N. Kollie, who claimed that the LDEA chief received benefits from individuals connected to an alleged cocaine trafficking network.

In a lengthy social media post, Kollie further alleged that George Wha Harris, also known as Leroy Harris, who has been charged in connection with an ongoing narcotics investigation, maintained relationships with senior security officials, including Biago.

The allegations have since circulated widely on social media and other platforms.

However, in a press release issued Friday, August 7, the LDEA described the claim as false, maintaining that it has not been supported by any verifiable evidence.

The Agency said Biago, who serves as a Deputy Commissioner of Police, categorically denies receiving or accepting the vehicle described in the allegation. According to the LDEA, he also did not authorize anyone to receive the vehicle on his behalf.

“The LDEA is not aware of any credible record, documentation, or evidence substantiating the claim,” the Agency said.

The drug enforcement agency acknowledged that public officials must remain subject to legitimate scrutiny, while urging anyone with credible evidence of misconduct to submit it to the appropriate investigative authorities for independent investigation.

“The LDEA recognizes that public officials must remain open to legitimate scrutiny. For that reason, any person possessing credible evidence of misconduct is encouraged to submit it to the appropriate investigative authority for an independent and lawful review,” the statement said.

The Agency emphasized that serious allegations should be tested against evidence and due process rather than repeated as established facts without verification.

The LDEA also reaffirmed its “zero tolerance” policy toward corruption, misconduct and collusion with criminal networks, stressing that the standard applies to every officer regardless of rank.

“These standards apply to every officer, regardless of rank, and any substantiated violation will be addressed in accordance with law and established disciplinary procedures,” the Agency said.

The LDEA further appealed to the public and media to verify allegations before publishing or sharing them, particularly when unsubstantiated claims could prejudice ongoing investigations, damage reputations or undermine public confidence in national security institutions.

The Agency clarified that its call for verification is not intended to restrict lawful criticism or responsible journalism, but rather to reinforce what it described as the shared responsibility to distinguish allegations from established facts.

As Liberia intensifies its efforts to combat drug trafficking, the LDEA urged members of the public to continue reporting suspicious activities through its hotlines: 0777-133-333 / 0888-133-333.

World.title: How a Paynesville Nightspot Became Ground Zero in Liberia’s Cocaine Case
World.content:
Monrovia – The operation that shut down Private Bar on Wednesday looked, from the outside, like a raid built to send a message. Heavily armed security officers blocked access to the premises as investigators moved through the property, and journalists who arrived at the scene were kept at a distance on the instructions of a senior female LDEA officer overseeing the operation. It was a markedly different posture than the one authority took just weeks earlier at a raid in the VOA Community connected to the same case, where two foreign nationals were arrested and reporters were allowed considerably closer access to observe. The contrast has not gone unnoticed, and it has renewed the same question that has followed this investigation since it began: why does transparency around this case seem to expand and contract depending on which door investigators are standing behind?

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Management’s own account of the closure raises a more pointed question still. In a notice issued after the operation, the company said that, to the best of its knowledge, it had not been served with any court order or other written legal directive authorizing the closure before the action was taken — a claim that, if accurate, would mean one of the most consequential steps taken in this investigation happened without the paperwork usually required to justify it. Authorities have not responded publicly to that claim and have declined to explain the legal basis for the closure or confirm whether a search warrant was obtained.

Chairs, Crates of Guinness, and Armed Officers

For several hours on Wednesday, the venue that has spent years hosting Paynesville’s nightlife and gaming crowds instead hosted investigators. Workers moved chairs, tables and crates of Guinness and other beverages inside the building as the search continued around them, an oddly domestic scene playing out under the watch of armed security. Employees were questioned. Documents were examined, their relevance to the drug case left unexplained. By the time the search wound down, the bar remained under guard, its usual evening crowd replaced by uniforms and uncertainty.

Police have not disclosed whether Harris himself was arrested during or after the operation, an omission that has left his legal status genuinely unclear even as the business tied to his name sits closed and guarded. That kind of ambiguity tends to fill in on its own in a city following a scandal this closely — and by Wednesday evening, plenty of speculation had rushed in to fill the space where an official explanation should have been.

“We Remain a Law-Abiding Business”

Private Bar’s management did not stay silent. In a notice addressed to employees and customers, the company struck a tone that was part reassurance, part legal caution, and part plea for patience:

“The Management of Private Sports Bar & Restaurant wishes to inform all our employees and valued customers that we remain a law-abiding business and are fully cooperating with the relevant authorities. The company respects the rule of law and the constitutional principle that every person is entitled to due process. As such, we will not comment on the merits of the ongoing investigation involving Mr. Harris, as the matter is currently before the appropriate legal authorities.”

The notice went on to describe the day’s inspection in specific terms, framing it as the latest in a pattern rather than an isolated discovery: “This morning, at approximately 10:00 a.m., the Joint Security Team conducted a thorough inspection of our premises, both inside and outside the bar. No illegal substances were found during the inspection. This was the third inspection since May, and on each occasion, no illegal substances have been discovered on our premises.”

On the closure itself, management was more pointed, stopping just short of calling the action unlawful while making clear it intends to find out whether it was: “Regarding the closure of our business today, Management wishes to state that, to the best of its knowledge, the company was not served with any court order or other written legal directive authorizing the closure before the action was taken. The company is consulting legal counsel to determine its rights and to seek appropriate clarification through the lawful processes available under the laws of the Republic of Liberia.” The notice closed by asking employees and customers for calm and patience, expressing confidence in the justice system, and promising the bar would reopen “as soon as possible.”



How a Nightlife Spot Became a Person of Interest

None of this explains, on its own, how a Paynesville entertainment venue ended up at the center of an international cocaine investigation — and authorities have offered little to fill that gap. What is publicly known traces back to the aftermath of the July 21 seizure of 3,971 kilograms of cocaine, worth an estimated $317 million, intercepted near Roberts International Airport in Duazon. According to prosecutors, Harris contacted several security and law enforcement officials in the hours after that seizure, allegedly attempting to facilitate the release of the shipment, and allegedly offered substantial sums of money to influence the outcome. He now faces a lengthy list of charges: drug trafficking, money laundering, economic sabotage, unlicensed importation and possession of illicit drugs, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, and criminal solicitation.

What investigators have not explained is the mechanism — whether the bar itself allegedly served as a meeting point for the network, a financial conduit for moving money, or something else entirely. What the breadth of the charges suggests, prosecutors’ own case implies, is that they view Harris as someone who allegedly facilitated transactions and coordinated contacts central to the operation, not as a bystander who simply happened to own a business connected to the wrong people. Whether the bar’s own walls hold any evidence of that, three inspections turning up nothing would seem to argue against — though investigators, so far, appear unwilling to let that record settle the question.

The Company He Kept

Part of what has kept investigators’ attention fixed on Private Bar, beyond the allegations tied directly to Harris, is who else has been known to walk through its doors. Harris is said to have strong ties to Michael Brown, one of several individuals charged in connection with this investigation — Brown among those facing prosecution in absentia, not yet in custody alongside the others already before the courts. That relationship, according to people familiar with the case, is part of why a Paynesville bar owner’s name surfaced at all in an investigation that began with a cargo seizure at an airport many miles away: Private Bar was not simply a business Harris happened to own while unrelated events unfolded around him. By multiple accounts, the venue was a regular gathering spot for a number of those now accused of ties to the network, a detail that reframes the bar less as an incidental backdrop to the case and more as a place where the people at the center of it were known to spend their evenings.

None of that has been laid out in the formal charges made public so far, and Harris’s own alleged conduct — the calls to officials, the offers of money — remains the more direct thread connecting him to the July 21 seizure. But the overlap in social circles helps explain why investigators moved on the bar itself rather than simply pursuing Harris as an individual, and why a third inspection in three months, even one that turned up nothing, was not enough to keep the doors open.

What Happens to the Building Now

For now, Private Bar sits closed, guarded, and waiting — its future tied to a legal process that has, so far, moved with more force than explanation. Management says it is consulting counsel and hopes to reopen soon; the government has yet to say on what legal basis the doors were shut, or when, if ever, they’ll be allowed to open again. Somewhere between those two positions sits a business with employees owed paychecks, customers who used to fill its tables on a Wednesday night, and an owner whose fate in a courtroom will likely decide the bar’s fate long before any inspection does.

World.title: Liberia: Get to the Bottom of Private Bar — Before a Generation Pays the Price
World.content:
A nightspot closed for a day, its owner facing charges, and a lot of unanswered questions about who else spent their evenings there. If the government treats Private Bar as a single businessman’s problem rather than what it may actually be — a gathering place for a trafficking network operating in plain sight of Liberia’s young people — it will have missed the point of this entire scandal.

PRIVATE BAR ENTERTAINMENT CENTER is, on any ordinary night, exactly what its name promises: music, drinks, a crowd, mostly young. That is precisely what should worry Liberians most about what investigators now say was happening there. This newspaper reported this week that George “Leroy” Harris, the venue’s owner, faces a lengthy list of charges tied to the record $317 million cocaine seizure in Duazon, and that Harris is said to have strong ties to Michael Brown, one of several individuals charged in absentia in the broader case. By multiple accounts, Private Bar was a regular gathering spot for others accused of ties to the same network. Put plainly: a business built around Liberia’s young nightlife scene may have doubled, for some period of time, as a comfortable meeting ground for people allegedly moving hundreds of millions of dollars in cocaine through this country.

IF THAT IS TRUE, EVEN IN PART, the implications reach far beyond Harris’s own legal fate. A courtroom can settle what happens to one man. It cannot, by itself, answer the harder question this case raises: how many young Liberians spent evenings in that room, dancing a few tables away from the people now accused of running a trafficking operation, with no idea what they were standing next to? How many nights did a bar frequented by students, young professionals and Monrovia’s nightlife regulars double as an informal office for a cartel network? Those are not questions a single prosecution answers. They require an investigation into the venue itself — not just the man who owned it.

WE RECOGNIZE THE GOVERNMENT has already moved further than many expected. The closure this week, whatever questions remain about its legal basis, was a real step, and the charges against Harris are serious ones. But a single day’s closure and a management notice promising cooperation are not the same thing as a full accounting of what actually happened inside that building, over what period of time, and how many other establishments across Monrovia may be operating the same way, hiding in plain sight behind loud music and a young crowd that has no reason to suspect what’s really going on around them. Three prior inspections at Private Bar reportedly found no illegal substances on the premises. That should not be read as exoneration. Cartels do not store their product on the dance floor; they use spaces like this one to build relationships, pass information, and move money, precisely because a bar’s ordinary chaos gives them cover. A clean inspection tells you nothing about what was said in a back booth or arranged over a round of drinks.

THIS IS WHERE THE STAKES STOP being abstract. Liberia’s young people are already living through a summer in which cocaine has moved through their country’s main airport in industrial quantities, in which police commanders allegedly escorted the drugs themselves, and in which the institutions meant to protect them have repeatedly turned out to be entangled in the very crisis they were supposed to prevent. If the places where young Liberians go to relax and socialize are also, even occasionally, where trafficking networks conduct their business, then this is no longer only a law-enforcement problem. It is a public health and social problem, one that risks normalizing proximity to organized crime for an entire generation before anyone in government has fully reckoned with how deep it runs. A young person who spends enough nights in rooms where this kind of money and influence moves freely does not need to break a single law to be shaped by what they’ve witnessed.

THE BOAKAI ADMINISTRATION owes the country more than a closed bar and a set of charges against one man. It owes Liberians a genuine investigation into Private Bar’s role in this network — who else was present, how long this arrangement is believed to have run, whether other venues across the city have served the same purpose, and what, if anything, government regulators and licensing bodies knew or should have known before this scandal forced the issue into public view. It also owes young Liberians something less tangible but no less important: an honest public accounting of what happened in a space many of them walked through without a second thought, so that trust in the places they gather is not left to quietly erode along with trust in everything else this scandal has touched. Liberia cannot prosecute its way out of a problem it has not fully investigated. Get to the bottom of Private Bar — all the way to the bottom — before the cost of not knowing falls on people who never should have had to pay it.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai On Drug Scandal – ‘We Will Find You’ – But Will The Courts Deliver?
World.content:
He came to swear in judges and court marshals. He left having delivered the most direct public warning of his presidency — to drug traffickers, yes, but also, if the words are taken at face value, to anyone inside his own government still hoping this scandal blows over quietly.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – President Joseph Boakai’s remarks began, as these ceremonies usually do, with the formalities — congratulations to the new judges and court marshals, praise for the judiciary’s constitutional independence, gratitude to Joint Security personnel working “under difficult conditions.” And then, without much warning, the tone shifted into something closer to a direct address to an unseen audience. “To those who seek to bring illegal drugs into Liberia to destroy the lives of our young people, hear me today!” Boakai said. “To those who believe Liberia can be used as a transit point for international narcotics trafficking, hear me well! To those who believe their position, influence, wealth, or authority places them beyond the reach of justice, clean your ears and hear me today, well, well, and be warned!”

What followed was the kind of line that tends to outlive the speech itself. “We will identify you! We will pursue you! We will find you! And we will deal with you in accordance with the law,” Boakai said, before delivering the sentence his office will likely be held to for the rest of his term: “There will be no sacred cows in this Joseph Nyuma Boakai Administration.”

A Speech for Judges, Aimed at Everyone

The setting mattered as much as the words. Boakai chose a courtroom commissioning ceremony, not a security briefing or a press conference, to deliver his sharpest language yet on the drug scandal — a venue that let him frame the fight against trafficking as fundamentally a rule-of-law problem rather than only a policing one. “A nation cannot prosper where the rule of law is weak,” he told the incoming judges and marshals. “Investors lose confidence. Citizens lose hope. Criminals become emboldened.
